title: Travel light (Mark 6:7–13)
hook: he sends them out two by two with a staff and no bag

segments.voice: Yesterday, without honor at home: Nazareth looked at Jesus and asked, isn't this the carpenter? Did you see someone old in a new way? Day one hundred eighty-one.

Think about the last time you packed for a trip. The charger, the spare charger, the just-in-case sweater, snacks, a book you won't read. Most of us pack for every disaster we can imagine. Right after his own hometown turns him away, Jesus does something bold. He doesn't pull back. He multiplies. He sends the twelve out, in pairs, to the villages, to do what he's been doing. And before they go, he gives them a packing list. It's the shortest packing list in history. Today: travel light.
screen: `THE JUST-IN-CASE SWEATER.` → `SENT OUT IN PAIRS.` → `THE SHORTEST PACKING LIST.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old King James Bible: "take nothing for their journey, save a staff only; no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse: But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats." A staff, for walking and for dogs. Sandals. One coat. That's it. A scrip was a traveler's bag, the kind a wandering beggar or a street philosopher carried for collecting food. No bag means no stockpiling. They'll eat what they're given. Which means they have to be received. That's the point. Travelers without supplies depend on hospitality, and hospitality was sacred in that world. Jesus tells them: when a house takes you in, stay there. Don't shop around for a better one. And if a place won't have you, shake the dust off your feet as you leave, and move on. No grudges carried out of town either. Why two by two? Nobody walks alone. And in Jewish law, a matter was confirmed by two witnesses. So they go, and Mark says they preached that people should turn around and start again, drove out demons, and "anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them." Only Mark mentions the oil. Many churches still anoint the sick with oil, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians count it among the sacraments. One more detail: Mark lets them take a staff. Matthew and Luke say, not even a staff. Scholars have puzzled over it for centuries. Either way, the list is short on purpose. Less in the bag means more need for each other, and more room for trust.
screen: `A STAFF, SANDALS, ONE COAT.` · `NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.` · `STAY WHERE YOU'RE WELCOMED.` · `ANOINTED WITH OIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one thing out of your bag. Settle, and breathe. Picture your bag, backpack, purse, or pockets. What do you carry every day just in case? Then go deeper: what else are you carrying? A worry you pack every morning. A grudge. A plan B for a plan B. Choose one thing, one object or one weight, that you could leave behind today. Picture setting it down. If you pray, you can hand it to God. After the bell, actually take something out. The bell holds the time.
Travel light. The twelve sent out in pairs with a staff, sandals and one coat, depending on welcome.
Your line: travel light. Today, carry one thing less, in your bag or in your head, and notice who you lean on instead. Day one hundred eighty-one.

original.note: Greek: a leather bag for provisions, the kind wandering beggars carried. The King James calls it a scrip.

trapdoor: what you thought: advice about packing.
what it means: the twelve go out in pairs with almost nothing, so they depend on welcome, and on each other.
what a scholar hears: Mark allows a staff and sandals; Matthew and Luke forbid the staff. a small difference readers have long puzzled over.
